City, N.J. — The turkey was cooked. The drinks were poured. The bay was surging up the street. All that there was left for Dave Agrrera and his family to do this Thanksgiving was settle in on the porch and watch dislodged docks float down Bay Avenue.","type":"text"},{"content":"“We were just sitting around eating and drinking, watching the tide come in,” said Agrrera, who is 70, and lives year-round in Ocean City with his wife and daughter. “We just watched the docks flip down the road.”","type":"text"},{"content":"Thanksgiving was a day to ride out a storm the likes of which many hadn’t seen since Superstorm Sandy. Friday was a day to pick up the pieces.","type":"text"},{"content":"Thursday’s nor’easter battered the Jersey Shore with hurricane-force wind gusts and tidal flooding that swamped streets, knocked out power to thousands, disrupted holiday travel, damaged property, and chewed up beaches.","type":"text"},{"content":"Atlantic City suffered its worst coastal flooding since Sandy roared ashore in 2012. As the bay spilled into low-lying neighborhoods, emergency crews carried out 14 rescues, officials said. ","type":"text"},{"content":"The fast-moving storm ate away as much as 30% of the city’s remaining dunes, <a href=\"https://6abc.com/post/cleanup-begins-coastal-storm-brings-widespread-flooding-wind-damage-beach-erosion-jersey-shore/20090562/\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"\"><u>Atlantic City Emergency Management Chief Scott Evans told 6abc</u></a>. Between damage from Thanksgiving and an earlier nor’easter in September, <a href=\"https://www.inquirer.com/south-jersey/thanksgiving-storm-flooding-dunes-beach-erosion-20261127.html\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"\" title=\"https://www.inquirer.com/south-jersey/thanksgiving-storm-flooding-dunes-beach-erosion-20261127.html\">Shore mayors were left confronting their beaches’ futures</a> by the week’s end. ","type":"text"},{"content":"“Almost like Sandy,” said Peter McDonald, 57, sipping a Coors Friday afternoon at the Back Bay Ale House, a North Inlet institution since 2003 that overlooks the fishing boats of historic Gardner’s Basin. In the shadows of the casinos, the waterfront pub sits smack in one of Atlantic City’s most flood-prone neighborhoods.","type":"text"},{"content":"“The water was almost up to my waist,” said McDonald, who lives across from the bay. Downed street signs and toppled traffic signals still littered the city’s streets.","type":"text"},{"type":"image"},{"content":"The region still saw light rain Friday, adding slightly to the overall rainfall total of between one and four inches across the region. The Shore counties in South Jersey and Sussex County, Delaware, saw much higher precipitation levels than anywhere else.","type":"text"},{"content":"Most of Philadelphia itself saw less than two inches of rain. By contrast, Cape May County saw 5.1 inches of rain reported in Southwest Ocean View.","type":"text"},{"content":"Stubborn power outages remained in pockets of the region. As of Friday afternoon, Peco reported more than 1,000 active outages with nearly 22,000 customers impacted. That’s compared to the 225,000 customers who lost power at some point on Thanksgiving Day, numbers the energy company shared at a news conference Friday.","type":"text"},{"content":"Parts of the U.S. clean up, power outages being restored after Thanksgiving storm soaks East Coast","type":"interstitial_link"},{"content":"Atlantic City Electric reported active outages Friday afternoon, with more than 9,400 customers impacted. In the South Jersey counties closer to Philadelphia, PSE&G reported nearly 300 active outages, with about 4,300 customers affected. ","type":"text"},{"content":"As the Delaware River approached high tide again Friday afternoon, the National Weather Service reported the possibility of one more round of further flooding.","type":"text"},{"content":"“We still have one more high tide cycle on the Delaware River that will get to coastal flooding thresholds,” said Sarah Johnson, spokesperson for the National Weather Service. “But then after that, we should be done.”","type":"text"},{"type":"image"},{"content":"Johnson reported that there was some lingering tidal flooding in some back bays, like Barnegat Bay, and that Philadelphia is already above minor flood thresholds. ","type":"text"},{"content":"The inclement weather isn’t quite done with the Philadelphia region. Another storm system is expected to hit late Sunday and into Monday, with more rain expected. ","type":"text"},{"content":"This second storm will only be an echo of Thursday’s extravaganza. The National Weather Service only expects a half-inch to an inch of rain, with peak wind speeds on Monday of 45 miles per hour. ","type":"text"},{"content":"“That’s strong, but quite a far cry from what we saw from the storm system yesterday,” Johnson said. ","type":"text"},{"content":"Recovery down the Shore","type":"header"},{"content":"Along the Jersey Shore, recovery efforts are underway as the full effects of Thanksgiving’s storm are still being tabulated. ","type":"text"},{"content":"Ocean City, celebrated for its iconic boardwalk and eight-mile stretch of wide, well-groomed beaches, bore an especially heavy burden. Winds hit 70 mph. Tides flirted with record highs. In parts of the island, the water was more than knee-deep. The water rose 19 inches in Agrrera’s garage, located on high ground in the north end. He counted himself among the lucky ones.","type":"text"},{"content":"Mim Schreck and Anne Morrissey decided to beat the storm to Thanksgiving. The friends, who live on nearby Fourth Street with their pup, Linc, and once ran a popular Asbury Avenue boutique, cooked and ate their Thanksgiving dinner on Wednesday, fearing the coming storm would knock out their power.","type":"text"},{"type":"image"},{"type":"image"},{"content":"It didn’t. But the winds shook the house. And the water rose nearly two feet at Fourth and Simpson, a notorious trouble spot for flooding, where locals sometimes kayak during storms. September’s nor’easter was nothing compared to Thursday, the women said.","type":"text"},{"content":"“Full moon, high tide, and high winds,” Schreck said, surveying her sodden garage and drowned blueberry gardens and shrubs. “You put those together, and there’s nothing you can do.”","type":"text"},{"content":"The double-stacked sandbags outside their garage proved no match for the relentless water, said Morrissey. At times Thursday, the winds seemed as violent as when Sandy roared ashore in 2012, she said.","type":"text"},{"content":"Like other Ocean City residents, wielding brooms and mops Friday, Morrissey credited the city with making strides in recent years to combat flooding. Thursday laid bare how much work remains, they said.","type":"text"},{"content":"Erick Giunta, 36, moved into a home near the bay in August with his wife and two young children. Six inches of water swamped his first floor Thursday, leaving upward of $10,000 in damage, he said. He’ll tackle much of the cleanup himself, with borrowed equipment from friends. He wishes the city would help residents with basics, like sandbags and dehumidifiers.","type":"text"},{"content":"“There’s just little things they could do to potentially help people better prepare,” he said.","type":"text"},{"content":"Ocean City mayor Jay Gillian did not respond to a request for comment Friday.","type":"text"},{"content":"Little could have prepared Zach Spears, 42, of Fishtown, for the deep water that seemed to swallow his car at the foot of the Ninth Street Bridge, which spans Great Egg Harbor Bay. Spears, who had come to Ocean City Thursday with his wife and toddler son to spend Thanksgiving with family, took refuge with them in an island Acme for nearly three hours, waiting for the waters to recede.","type":"text"},{"content":"“They were very nice,” he said of the supermarket staff. “I got some Hot Wheels for my kid.”","type":"text"},{"content":"With high tide Friday morning, the water came for some of the island’s streets again, creeping in from the bay and ocean and welling up through storm drains. Maureen Boyle, a retiree from Mayfair, who lives in Ocean City’s South End, watched as water that had lingered overnight began climbing again, before finally ebbing.","type":"text"},{"content":"At the height of Thursday’s storm, debris flew through the air like something out of a disaster movie, she said. Her condo had escaped largely unscathed. Like many on the island, she felt lucky.","type":"text"},{"content":"Boyle had considered a daughter’s house in Egg Harbor Township Thursday, before deciding to hunker down. “It was scary,” she said. ","type":"text"},{"content":"“By the time you decide you want to go, it’s too late. ","type":"text"},{"content":"The then 26-year-old enrolled in a small, early-stage Jefferson Health trial of a novel vaccine. Designed to train the immune system to recognize and attack cancer cells, the treatment gave her hope that, if the cancer were to return, her body would know to eliminate it.","type":"text"},{"content":"That’s the idea behind so-called cancer vaccines, a rapidly evolving field seeing progress in several clinical trials this year after decades of setbacks. ","type":"text"},{"content":"The first late-stage trial success for an mRNA cancer vaccine came in August for a melanoma vaccine developed by pharmaceutical giants Merck and Moderna. And this month, New York-headquartered company SELLAS Life Sciences <a href=\"https://www.washingtonpost.com/health/2026/11/17/leukemia-vaccine-passes-key-trial-adding-breakthrough-year-cancer-drugs/\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"\" title=\"https://www.washingtonpost.com/health/2026/11/17/leukemia-vaccine-passes-key-trial-adding-breakthrough-year-cancer-drugs/\">announced positive results</a> in an advanced cancer vaccine trial involving 126 leukemia patients.","type":"text"},{"content":"Penn helped test a promising mRNA cancer vaccine. Here’s what the trial means for the field.","type":"interstitial_link"},{"content":"Experts believe the technology may work best when cancer is caught early or after other treatments have already removed tumors.","type":"text"},{"content":"Some early cancer vaccine trials failed when they were tested as standalone treatments in patients with advanced cancer, who tend to have significant disease and weakened immune systems. Other candidates used targets also present on healthy tissue, weakening the body’s ability to generate an immune response.","type":"text"},{"content":"“I think there’s a potential for vaccines in virtually every type of cancer — the key being the ability to get those vaccines into patients when their immune system is still robust,” Ben Stanger, director of the Penn Pancreatic Cancer Research Center, said.","type":"text"},{"content":"Jefferson’s trial is just one example of a cancer vaccine being developed and tested locally. The University of Pennsylvania’s Susan Domchek is leading trials testing whether vaccines can prevent cancer in people with BRCA genetic mutations, which increase their risk of certain cancers.","type":"text"},{"content":"Penn’s BRCA cancer vaccine trial aims to prevent the disease in healthy people","type":"interstitial_link"},{"content":"Many of these efforts remain in the early stages, meaning it will still take years to prove safety and efficacy. Most novel treatments do not make it to the point where they gain approval and become widely available to patients.","type":"text"},{"content":"Across 46 patients in the Jefferson trial whose gastrointestinal cancers were previously surgically removed, the vaccine was found to be safe, according to <a href=\"https://ascopubs.org/doi/10.1200/JCO.2026.44.16_suppl.3617\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"\" title=\"https://ascopubs.org/doi/10.1200/JCO.2026.44.16_suppl.3617\">an abstract presented at the American Society of Clinical Oncology</a> (ASCO) annual meeting in late May. ","type":"text"},{"content":"The results are preliminary and have not yet gone through the rigorous peer review process usually required for publication in an academic journal. ","type":"text"},{"content":"The tested vaccine also induced robust immune responses in patients who received the highest dose, suggesting it could provoke, and hopefully train, the immune system. However, its effect on cancer remains unproven.","type":"text"},{"content":"Since the trial was not randomized and controlled — the gold standard for establishing causation — it cannot be used to evaluate efficacy.","type":"text"},{"content":"“It needs a larger, better-powered study with a control group,” said Stanger, who was not involved in the trial.","type":"text"},{"content":"The Jefferson team said it was too early to determine the cost of the vaccine.","type":"text"},{"content":"Johnson doesn’t know whether the vaccine helped her. But she was happy she received the strongest dose, believing it could give her the best chance of benefiting.","type":"text"},{"content":"The 30-year-old Manayunk resident remains cancer-free and is expected to give birth next month to her first child. ","type":"text"},{"content":"“We live a very happy, healthy, fortunate life with a lot of friends and family around us,” she said of her life post-cancer.","type":"text"},{"type":"image"},{"content":"The potential","type":"header"},{"content":"When people think of a vaccine, they usually picture shots for the flu or COVID-19.","type":"text"},{"content":"These train the immune system to recognize and fight off a virus if exposed. Cancer vaccines are much the same. By teaching the body to recognize a particular target on cancer cells, the technology helps prepare the immune system to fend off threats. ","type":"text"},{"content":"Think of it like arming the immune system with wanted posters of suspected criminals.","type":"text"},{"content":"“When it comes to vaccines, the immune system is the drug,” Stanger said.","type":"text"},{"content":"However, cancer vaccines in trials are more often being deployed after cancer is already diagnosed. ","type":"text"},{"content":"For example, the novel melanoma vaccine was used to prevent cancer from recurring in people after initial treatment. The same goes for the leukemia trial.","type":"text"},{"content":"“We traditionally think of vaccines as something that you give before you get an illness,” Domchek said. “And suddenly we’re using the word vaccine for things that are considered treatments.”","type":"text"},{"content":"The Penn researcher wondered whether the label “immune therapy” should be used instead to avoid confusion. Her BRCA cancer vaccine approach, by contrast, is trying to prevent cancer from developing in the first place.","type":"text"},{"content":"Approaches have ranged from personalized therapies to off-the-shelf products<b> </b>that are premade and standardized.","type":"text"},{"content":"In the melanoma trial, patients’ individual tumors were sequenced to identify targets for the personalized vaccines. ","type":"text"},{"content":"Meanwhile, Domchek’s trial focuses on patients whose BRCA mutations elevate their risk but who don’t yet have cancer. A personalized approach won’t work “because they don’t have something to sequence,” Domchek said.","type":"text"},{"content":"The Jefferson vaccine uses a target shared across patients with gastrointestinal tumors.","type":"text"},{"content":"The benefits of an off-the-shelf therapy are its scalability, immediate availability, and potentially lower manufacturing costs. A personalized approach offers greater adaptability, precision, and specificity.","type":"text"},{"content":"“There’s going to be a role for both, for sure,” Eileen O’Reilly, a medical oncologist at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York not involved in either local effort, said of the two approaches.","type":"text"},{"content":"Cancer vaccines can be delivered in different ways, from the mRNA technology built on Nobel Prize-winning research at Penn to virus-based platforms.","type":"text"},{"content":"If successful, cancer vaccines could offer a lasting advantage compared to other treatments.","type":"text"},{"content":"“When responses happen, they have the potential for durability,” O’Reilly said.","type":"text"},{"content":"Penn effort continues","type":"header"},{"type":"image"},{"content":"BRCA carriers are at elevated risk of developing cancers involving the breasts, ovaries, pancreas, prostate, and skin.","type":"text"},{"content":"That creates a unique challenge for scientists seeking a target shared across tumor types and patients. A universal vaccine for all cancers is considered unlikely because cancer encompasses many different diseases.","type":"text"},{"content":"The approach being tested at Penn vaccinates patients against three common features of cancers.","type":"text"},{"content":"One is a subunit of an enzyme called telomerase that appears in larger amounts than typical in 95% of human cancers. The others are WT1, a protein found in a range of cancers, and PSMA, a protein largely found in prostate cancer.","type":"text"},{"content":"Vaccines with multiple targets could prove more robust given that cancers are highly complex and adaptive, said O’Reilly, who is developing a novel pancreatic cancer vaccine at Memorial Sloan Kettering that<b> </b>targets several common genetic drivers of cancer. ","type":"text"},{"content":"However, researchers will need to determine whether having multiple targets dilutes the overall quality of the immune response.","type":"text"},{"content":"“If you have multiple different targets, are you limiting what the immune response can do?” O’Reilly said.","type":"text"},{"content":"Domchek’s Phase 1b trial is testing the vaccine in 44 participants: 28 who are healthy with no prior cancer, and 16 who are cancer-free but have a history of the disease. Early findings reported <a href=\"https://ascopubs.org/doi/10.1200/JCO.2025.43.16_suppl.10505?referrer=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.google.com%2F\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"\" title=\"https://ascopubs.org/doi/10.1200/JCO.2025.43.16_suppl.10505?referrer=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.google.com%2F\">in 2025 at the ASCO annual meeting</a> showed the vaccine was safe.","type":"text"},{"content":"The technology uses bits of DNA delivered into cells via an electric jolt.","type":"text"},{"content":"Her team is next looking at whether the vaccine generated an adequate immune response before they move on to trials testing its efficacy against cancer.","type":"text"},{"content":"“We still have a ways to go because we have to prove that it decreases cancer risk,” she said.","type":"text"},{"content":"Jefferson’s vaccine trial","type":"header"},{"type":"image"},{"content":"Drew Weissman, one of the Nobel Prize-winning mRNA scientists at Penn, doesn’t think cancer vaccines would work well in someone whose advanced cancer cannot be removed. The immune system has a hard time killing large tumors, he explained to The Inquirer in a <a href=\"https://www.inquirer.com/health/penn-mrna-cancer-melanoma-vaccine-trial-potential-20260925.html\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"\" title=\"https://www.inquirer.com/health/penn-mrna-cancer-melanoma-vaccine-trial-potential-20260925.html\">September article</a>.","type":"text"},{"content":"That’s part of why Jefferson’s approach targets patients who have already had their tumors surgically removed.","type":"text"},{"content":"The vaccine, delivered using a virus, targets a protein called GUCY2C commonly found<b> </b>on cancer cells in gastrointestinal tumors.","type":"text"},{"content":"Forty-six patients all received the treatment, with most reporting flulike side effects. For Johnson, that meant a high fever and symptoms that lasted for about two to three days.","type":"text"},{"content":"Among the 21 patients with colorectal cancer included in the analysis, higher vaccine doses were associated with lower rates of cancer recurrence at two years.","type":"text"},{"content":"“We are seeing an earlier hint of preventing the recurrences in high-risk patients, and our next step is to prove that,” said Babar Bashir, the Jefferson oncologist who led the trial alongside Adam Snook, the Jefferson scientist who developed the technology.","type":"text"},{"content":"Stanger said it is hard to tell whether the reported decrease in relapse is meaningful, since there was no control group and the study was small. ","type":"text"},{"content":"O’Reilly agreed, noting that without randomization, there can be “enormous selection bias” in how patients are chosen.","type":"text"},{"content":"The Jefferson team is preparing for a follow-up Phase 2b trial, funded by a roughly $2 million grant from the Pennsylvania Department of Health.","type":"text"}],"credits":{"by":[{"_id":"yup_kayla","description":"I write stories about scientific research, medicine, and medical education.","name":"Kayla Yup","url":"https://www.inquirer.com/author/yup_kayla/"}]},"description":{"basic":"Researchers at Jefferson and Penn are developing vaccines designed to train the immune system to recognize and attack cancer cells. December 1776.</b>","type":"text"},{"content":"The American Revolution is on the brink of collapse. And George Washington knows it. He trembles for Philadelphia.","type":"text"},{"content":"Washington, 44, writes by wavering candlelight in the borrowed rooms of a stately stone mansion. He wishes to heaven his quill could convey a more favorable tale. The general is on the run. The British have blasted him from his fortifications in New York and chased him clear across New Jersey, over the Delaware River into Pennsylvania. His soldiers are sick and starving and disappearing. The Revolution is coming apart. ","type":"text"},{"content":"George Washington is fighting to keep his army alive.","type":"text"},{"type":"image"},{"content":"In Philadelphia, not 30 miles away, the citizenry has calculated the grim arithmetic. An estimated 15,000 Philadelphians — roughly half the city — flees for Bucks and Chester Counties, or to Delaware and Maryland. Even the Congress, conspiring at the State House at Sixth and Chestnut, reconvenes in Baltimore.","type":"text"},{"content":"The birthplace of American independence can be mistaken for a ghost town. Martial law prevails. Schools are closed. Shops are shuttered. Wagons piled high with worldly possessions of fleeing families clog roads out of town. Wild rumors circulate that Washington would sooner burn Philadelphia than let the city fall into British hands. Scant city militia dig in.","type":"text"},{"content":"The great general is reduced to hiding boats. His bedraggled men have spent days seizing or destroying every vessel they can find along the Jersey banks. Anything to keep the British from crossing the Delaware.","type":"text"},{"content":"Washington needs men. The ones he has are counting the days until they can go home. His second in command — the ambitious, scheming Gen. Charles Lee — has managed to get himself captured at a Jersey tavern, miles from his troops. ","type":"text"},{"content":"“Unhappy man!” Washington fumes in a letter to a cousin at Mount Vernon, his Virginia plantation. “Taken by his own imprudence!”","type":"text"},{"content":"And it is not just the army’s strength that is dwindling. It is the new nation’s will to fight. ","type":"text"},{"content":"In Jersey, people are flocking to the protection of the Crown. Washington finds little more fight in the countryside of Pennsylvania.","type":"text"},{"content":"“If this fails,” Washington writes of his hopes for fresh troops, letting the mask of command slip, “I think the game will be pretty well up.”","type":"text"},{"content":"A rare glimpse","type":"header"},{"content":"By winter 1776, the spirit that swept Philadelphia in July seems all but extinguished. George Washington — and the colonies — are on the ropes. The December 1776 Washington letter provides a <a href=\"https://founders.archives.gov/?q=%20Recipient%3A%22Washington%2C%20Lund%22%20Author%3A%22Washington%2C%20George%22&s=1111311111&r=36\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"\">rare glimpse of Washington at his lowest</a>.","type":"text"},{"content":"Now on display at the <a href=\"https://www.amrevmuseum.org/news/now-on-view-letter-from-george-washington\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"\">Museum of the American Revolution</a>, the relic marks 250 years since that winter of 1776, when a newly minted nation teetered on extinction. Dark days of rebellion, just before a remarkable turn of fortune: the Ten Crucial Days, when Washington and his ragtag army snatched improbable victories at Trenton and Princeton, reviving a dying cause. A reminder of how close it all came to ending before it had barely begun.","type":"text"},{"content":"“Washington is trying to escape annihilation by the British,” said Matthew Skic, director of collections and exhibitions at the museum. ","type":"text"},{"content":"“From Washington’s perspective, if the Continental Army is over and done with, the Revolution is over and done with.”","type":"text"},{"type":"image"},{"content":"Desperation pours through Washington’s elegant, looping script.","type":"text"},{"content":"“In short your imagination can scarce extend to a situation more distressing than mine,” Washington writes, before somehow turning to the mundane affairs of Mount Vernon, a refuge from war, perhaps.","type":"text"},{"content":"Last on display at Mount Vernon in 2006 — and remaining on display in the museum’s core exhibit through May 2027 — the letter reveals the stoic general at his rawest.","type":"text"},{"content":"“It’s a letter that epitomizes the darkest hour,” Skic said. “We consider this the low point.”","type":"text"},{"content":"Crucial days","type":"header"},{"content":"The general cannot know how close he is to reversing the fortunes of war. On Christmas night, his ragged army will close the icy Delaware in a stunning surprise raid. At Trenton, the general who could barely keep his army together will have breathed new life into a dying revolution. The 10 days ahead bring more victories and waves of reenlistments.","type":"text"},{"content":"“Those 10 crucial days are crucial because they essentially rescue the Revolution from total defeat within the first six months of the Declaration of Independence,” Skic said.","type":"text"},{"content":"1777 would hold triumphs and heartbreaks of its own. But the Revolution would continue. the dining room of a Montgomery County senior living community on an early November evening, a quiet reunion of old friends was taking shape.","type":"text"},{"content":"Over broiled fish and sweet carrots, they retold old stories, inquired about family, and debated the details of the historical events that shaped their pasts, some lost to the widening gulf of time between then and now.","type":"text"},{"content":"It was, however, no ordinary gathering.","type":"text"},{"content":"The group had assembled at the Foulkeways at Gwynedd senior living community on Nov. 9 to remember 1971, the year eight activists broke into an FBI satellite office in Media, stealing thousands of documents that would expose the agency’s extensive surveillance and harassment of American citizens. The burglary and ensuing revelations changed public opinion of the bureau and laid the groundwork for the first true oversight of America’s intelligence agencies.","type":"text"},{"content":"Seated around the dinner table were Keith Forsyth, one of the eight burglars; journalist Betty Medsger, who first broke the story of the stolen documents; civil rights attorney David Kairys, who was the burglars’ lawyer and friend for many years; and documentarian Johanna Hamilton, who produced a 2014 film about the burglary. ","type":"text"},{"content":"Fifty-five years after the burglary, and 12 years after Medsger and Hamilton released <a href=\"https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/224642/the-burglary-by-betty-medsger/\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"\">journalistic</a> <a href=\"https://1971film.com/\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"\">projects</a> that first revealed the burglars’ identities to the public, the four friends<b> </b>had assembled<b> </b>for a discussion and screening of Hamilton’s film. Hamilton traveled from London, and Medsger, from New York.","type":"text"},{"content":"They had gathered, too, to honor Kairys, 83, now battling Parkinson’s disease at Foulkeways. For decades, Kairys served as a prominent Philadelphia civil rights litigator and was a key source in the making of Hamilton’s film. ","type":"text"},{"content":"“So many times, I think people remember primarily that this group of ordinary people did this amazing thing,” said Medsger. “... We lose sight of both the historical significance in the end, but also, what motivated them?”","type":"text"},{"type":"image"},{"content":"Uncovering a campaign of surveillance","type":"header"},{"content":"On the evening of March 8, 1971,<b> </b>as the rest of the world was captivated by the heavyweight championship fight between Muhammad Ali and Joe Frazier, eight activists broke into the FBI’s satellite office in Media.","type":"text"},{"content":"Medsger, now 84, was a 29-year-old reporter when an envelope full of unfamiliar documents, mailed by the burglars, landed on her desk at the Washington Post. ","type":"text"},{"content":"She had <a href=\"https://www.washingtonpost.com/history/2021/09/01/fbi-burglary-hoover-cointelpro/\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"\" title=\"https://www.washingtonpost.com/history/2021/09/01/fbi-burglary-hoover-cointelpro/\">arrived at the Post</a><i> </i>a year earlier from the now-defunct <a href=\"https://www.inquirer.com/philly/business/20090602_Philadelphia_Bulletin_ceases_publication.html\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"\">Philadelphia Bulletin</a>, where, as a religion reporter, she’d profiled John Raines, a professor later revealed as one of the burglars, and covered Catholic anti-war activists. ","type":"text"},{"content":"Raines and his wife mailed the stolen documents to Medsger because they “thought Betty would take it seriously,” Bonnie Raines told the Post in 2021. ","type":"text"},{"content":"The documents, as reported by Medsger, revealed a widespread effort by American intelligence officers to monitor and subvert the activities of activists. ","type":"text"},{"content":"The FBI had <a href=\"https://www.delcotimes.com/2014/02/09/secrets-revealed-in-1971-burglary-of-fbi-office-in-media/\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"\">hired informants</a>, the documents revealed,<b> </b>to report on the activities of students and professors at local colleges, including Swarthmore, Haverford, <a href=\"https://www.nytimes.com/1971/04/13/archives/a-citizens-commission-writes-to-seven-persons-who-it-says-served-as.html\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"\">Lincoln University</a>, and Pennsylvania Military College (now Widener University). Every Black student at Swarthmore was being surveilled, as were members of the Black Students Union at Pennsylvania Military College. FBI agents had been <a href=\"https://www.washingtonpost.com/history/2024/06/26/ed-helms-podcast-snafu-fbi/\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"\">instructed</a> to “enhance the paranoia” in activist circles and “get the point across that there is an FBI agent behind every mailbox.” ","type":"text"},{"content":"Agents engaged in behavior ranging “from crude to cruel to life-threatening and murderous,” said Medsger, speaking on a panel before a large crowd of Foulkeways residents.","type":"text"},{"type":"image"},{"content":"Arguably the single most important file stolen was a cover sheet with the term “COINTELPRO” scrawled in the top right corner — later revealed to be the FBI’s sweeping program of monitoring and infiltrating groups it thought to be subversive, from Students for a Democratic Society<b> </b>and feminist organizations to the Black Panthers.","type":"text"},{"content":"Medsger’s story set off a flurry of media reports and laid the groundwork for the first permanent congressional oversight of intelligence agencies through the <a href=\"https://www.senate.gov/about/powers-procedures/investigations/church-committee.htm\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"\">Church Committee</a>, a 1975 Senate committee that investigated allegations of U.S. intelligence agents spying on American citizens. ","type":"text"},{"content":"Before the revelations from the stolen documents came to light, a “culture of protection” shielded intelligence agencies from accountability, Medsger said.","type":"text"},{"content":"“I think it’s important to understand that nobody knew how J. Edgar Hoover’s FBI operated,” she said. ”There was a huge public relations operation that had been in play for decades by 1971, and it just put out story after story about how great the FBI was.” ","type":"text"},{"content":"As the fallout from the burglary reshaped Americans’ relationships with the federal government, the burglars, who swore one another to secrecy, faded back into everyday life. For decades, they remained anonymous.","type":"text"},{"type":"image"},{"content":"It was 20-odd years after the burglary, at a dinner party at the Raines’ home, that John Raines revealed to Medsger his role in the crime.","type":"text"},{"content":"“John blurted out what he forever claimed he never intended to blurt out,” Medsger said. ","type":"text"},{"content":"Still, it wasn’t until 2014 — after Watergate and Iran-Contra, the MOVE bombing, 9/11, and the first Obama administration — that the burglars publicly revealed themselves in Medsger’s book, <i>The Burglary: The Discovery of J. Edgar Hoover’s Secret FBI</i>, as young Philadelphia-area anti-war activists. In a documentary directed and written by Hamilton that same year, five came forward by name.","type":"text"},{"content":"The statute of limitations had passed on the burglary after just five years, but rumors that the federal government wanted to charge the burglars with espionage kept them in the shadows for much longer, Medsger and Hamilton said.","type":"text"},{"content":"The burglars, who called themselves the Citizens’ Commission to Investigate the FBI, were led by prominent anti-war activist and Haverford College professor William “Bill” Davidon. Davidon, Forsyth, Bonnie and John Raines, and<b> </b>Bob Williamson<b> </b>revealed their identities in the 2014 book and film. Another burglar, <a href=\"https://www.inquirer.com/philly/blogs/attytood/Last-fugitive-from-1971-Media-FBI-burglary-goes-public.html\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"\">Judi Feingold</a>, came forward<b> </b>through Medsger the same year, and the remaining two burglars, <a href=\"https://www.sfchronicle.com/local/article/50-years-after-the-famous-FBI-office-burglary-16001070.php\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"\">Ralph Daniel</a> and <a href=\"https://www.washingtonpost.com/history/2024/06/26/ed-helms-podcast-snafu-fbi/\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"\">Sara Shumer</a>, have gone public more recently.","type":"text"},{"content":"The activists ranged in age from 19 to 43. Some were professors, others college dropouts, some young parents. Many had been involved in the anti-war activities that swept across Philadelphia throughout the 1960s.","type":"text"},{"type":"image"},{"content":"‘A lot has happened’ since","type":"header"},{"content":"At Foulkeways earlier this month, both speakers and attendees recounted a Philadelphia of decades past, one where FBI agents swarmed Powelton Village and draft board raids captivated the public consciousness.","type":"text"},{"content":"One resident of the Quaker-founded community recalled living in the Temple University home where Students for a Democratic Society held their meetings and worrying that the FBI had tapped their phones. Another said the Media burglary inspired him to request his own FBI file through the Freedom of Information Act, passed in 1966. A third resident remembered John Raines as the minister at her wedding and a “wonderful person.”","type":"text"},{"content":"Some asked Medsger, Hamilton, and Forsyth how they understand the burglary now, as the country’s Vietnam-era protesters age and the United States finds itself in a time of heightened anxiety around <a href=\"https://www.inquirer.com/news/license-plate-reader-pushback-flock-new-jersey-20260914.html\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"\" title=\"https://www.inquirer.com/news/license-plate-reader-pushback-flock-new-jersey-20260914.html\">surveillance and government overreach</a>.","type":"text"},{"content":"Medsger described today’s FBI under director Kash Patel as “an arm of retribution for the president.”","type":"text"},{"type":"image"},{"content":"Hamilton noted that nearly half of the funding for her film came from the Independent Television Service, funded by the Corporation for Public Broadcasting, an organization that <a href=\"https://www.nytimes.com/2026/01/05/business/media/corporation-for-public-broadcasting.html\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"\">ceased to exist</a> earlier this year after it was stripped of its federal funding.","type":"text"},{"content":"For Forsyth, now 76, who picked the lock of the FBI office during the 1971 burglary,<b> </b>while “things have definitely gone in the wrong direction” in recent years, the Vietnam-era mass surveillance and suppression of social movements would be unrecognizable to Americans today.","type":"text"},{"content":"It had been a long time since Hamilton had watched the film with an audience, making for an emotional experience for the filmmaker.","type":"text"},{"content":"“A lot has happened in the years since the film was finished,” Hamilton told the crowd, pausing to collect herself. ","type":"text"},{"content":"Davidon <a href=\"https://www.inquirer.com/philly/obituaries/20131118_William_C__Davidon__86__professor_and_peace_activist.html\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"\">died in 2013</a> at 86 from Parkinson’s disease during the filming of Hamilton’s documentary. John Raines <a href=\"https://www.inquirer.com/philly/obituaries/john-raines-84-civil-rights-activist-cleric-and-temple-prof-20171113.html\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"\">died in 2017</a> at 84. Williamson <a href=\"https://neptunesociety.com/obituaries/albuquerque-nm/robert-williamson-12891957\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"\">died in May</a> at 76.","type":"text"},{"content":"“It’s a privilege to be allowed into people’s lives,” Hamilton said, recalling the many conversations and visits with the burglars and their families that preceded the making of the film. "},{"_id":"JZ5ILMIYTRD6VFLBYEJFWXC6SM","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Trevor Zegras was officially elevated from the fourth line to alongside Denver Barkey and Owen Tippett, and Cole Knuble was dropped down with Sean Couturier and Noel Acciari. burden"},{"_id":"2NGGWKGBTNFDBHHOOHRGNXZSFY","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Last week, I wrote about one of our city’s biggest challenges: our stagnant and anemic economy. The lack of opportunity in Philadelphia is the <a href=\"https://www.pew.org/en/research-and-analysis/issue-briefs/2019/09/whos-leaving-philadelphia-and-why\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"\">biggest reason people leave</a> (and why we’re back to being America’s poorest big city)."},{"_id":"PCCYR6RTRNCOTEKGFNQOXH2LZE","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"This week, City Council held a hearing into one of the biggest <i>obstacles</i> to a stronger local economy: our onerous business taxes. The end of the <a href=\"https://www.phila.gov/media/20251028121348/Philadelphia-business-tax-changes-starting-in-FY26.pdf\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"\" title=\"https://www.phila.gov/media/20251028121348/Philadelphia-business-tax-changes-starting-in-FY26.pdf\">$100,000 exemption for small businesses</a> adds urgency to the discussion."},{"_id":"ZWYXOMFJDNHJLFGLLQ7MR32W3I","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"While many American cities tax employers, Philadelphia takes it to another level. A Philadelphia-based business pays $1.395 for every $1,000 in revenue produced within the city. The city then takes 5.65% of the business’ net income. The city also has a net profits tax, which charges 3.74% to residents and 3.43% to nonresidents."},{"_id":"F6HFJ4GTUBDRDOMKWTXHXGCBTE","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Beyond these costs, the city also charges a wage tax (with roughly the same rates as the net profits tax), a 2% additional sales tax, and various industry-specific fees like the sugary drinks tax, liquor by the drink tax, hotel tax, and parking tax."},{"_id":"7FVHVL3M7VC6XC7P6MS3TYUIIY","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"For decades, this system has helped drive employers out of the city and into the welcoming arms of Conshohocken, Plymouth Meeting, and Malvern. The exodus of jobs into the suburbs makes it harder for city residents to access opportunity and contributes to Philadelphia’s lack of economic mobility."},{"_id":"LBYL6NXHMJESHPTNXCE6W5SVCM","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Over the years, various tax commissions have returned with the same conclusion — we need to change this system. Meanwhile, city leaders have responded with an incremental approach."},{"_id":"NNBFP4VNNFGITE2WVRHAA4AKOE","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Over time, the tax rates go down, slightly, across the board. This has predictably made no one happy. The business community is still paying onerous rates, and progressive advocates lament the missing revenue."},{"_id":"W4IFE2432JBWDBJEZZFQFAIW2M","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"I would humbly suggest an alternative approach, one seemingly shared by Councilmember <b>Isaiah Thomas</b>. Instead of reducing all three tax rates at once, officials should focus on the net income portion, which is the most likely to determine where a company chooses to locate."},{"_id":"LDGUAMUK2ZHQNLKK6VVEWLPMIU","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"At the hearing, city officials suggested that this would be less equitable because more profitable companies would see the biggest benefit. But that perspective is backward. The goal of taxes isn’t to conform to someone’s theoretical definition of fairness; it is to raise the most revenue for important civic needs while having the least negative impact on our economy."},{"_id":"ZWYIUKXIYZBDLJNRLP6AFAEJYM","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"A firm moving from Center City to Cherry Hill is a bigger blow to equity than any tax cut. The companies that pay the most in net income are also the most able to pick up and move without losing access to their existing customers in the city."},{"_id":"4TEHCNNUQBBXVKFKNGHUOFX2GI","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Near the end of the hearing, Thomas quoted an unnamed former colleague who told him that City Council “does a good job making sure people are comfortable being poor, but we need to pull poor people out of poverty.”"},{"_id":"IT3ONCFSQZBXLAC7DXP6RFFPSQ","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Hopefully, more of his colleagues will make the same connection."},{"owner":{"sponsored":false,"id":"pmn"},"copyright":"© Copyright 2026 The Philadelphia Inquirer","address":{"locality":"Philadelphia","region":"PA"},"syndication":{"search":true,"external_distribution":true},"auth":{"1":"f1c8c8094a2423ebdc4210260488b3cb60a14c32dc68c498ab0a61dc1590dfaf"},"caption":"Mayor Cherelle L. Or, namely, that any challengers to Council’s 17 incumbents would have to pay an additional 7% anytime they take out a political ad."},{"_id":"YXRYVSYROFHOZODZ2XCRZDNIVY","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"The other theory involves the Philadelphia Activities Fund, the largely discretionary pool of money href=\"https://www.inquirer.com/politics/philadelphia/city-council-school-district-closure-uber-tax-parker-20260421.html\" target=\"_blank\" rel=\"\">rideshare tax proposal failed</a>, eliminating a potential source of revenue."},{"_id":"OFDFXG7FWJFOHNHXHRVP6VQQAU","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"Council members see the midyear transfer as a way to use the activities fund to These concerns are legitimate. Passing by Broad and Morris Streets on a December weekend evening will provide a quick education on how chaotic things can get."},{"_id":"NO6A6TRVAZERXGRHB7C2DEQRYM","additional_properties":{},"type":"text","content":"In response, some have proposed closing the block to traffic during its busiest times.
